structure.title: Act I, scenes 1–3 · Hungry citizens and a soldier's answer
structure.text: The first dispute concerns grain in Rome. Caius Martius meets citizens who suspect the wealthy of withholding food. War against the neighbouring Volscians gives him a public problem he knows how to solve far better than a quarrel over distribution.

structure.title: Act I, scene 4 – Act III · A decorated body seeks election
structure.text: The fighting at Corioles wins Martius a new name. To become consul he must present his wounds and ask ordinary citizens for their votes. The same public that values his military service wants the right to give its consent to his rule.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · Beyond the gates
structure.text: The conflict over office drives the hero into a new relation with his city and with the enemy commander who knows him best. Rome's safety eventually requires a kind of persuasion its armies and statesmen are poorly placed to deliver.

people.name: Volumnia
people.role: Mother and maker of a soldier
people.text: She measures a son's achievement in wounds, honours and public service. The values she taught him made him valuable to Rome. They also made it exceptionally hard for her to teach him how to ask a citizen politely for anything.

people.name: Menenius and the tribunes
people.role: Patrician intermediary and the people's officers
people.text: Menenius tries a story and a joke where Martius would use an insult. The tribunes know how to turn the candidate's contempt into a question about what powers the people are prepared to surrender.

people.name: Aufidius
people.text: Fighting Coriolanus gives him a peculiar intimacy with the Roman's strengths. Admiration and rivalry coexist long before political circumstances give the men occasion to test how much confidence either feeling deserves.

context.title: What it means to ask for voices
context.text: A Roman candidate appeals for popular consent. The citizen who can grant a voice can also question the person asking. That brief equality feels humiliating to a soldier accustomed to a chain of command.

notice.text: Who gets to explain a hungry body?
notice.why: Menenius tells a fable about the belly and the other members. Its elegance can make the commonwealth sound like one cooperative body, even as actual hungry people stand waiting for an answer about actual food.

notice.text: Compare showing wounds with describing them.
notice.why: Other people eagerly recount the blows Martius endured. He resists displaying the scars when voters can judge them. The struggle over who may interpret his body runs from a family celebration into public office.

opening: Rome's greatest soldier despises the citizens whose votes he needs. On the battlefield his courage is unquestionable; in public life he regards asking for approval as humiliation. His supporters want him to perform a little warmth, and his enemies know exactly how to provoke him. Shakespeare gives the city a defender who cannot bear the people he defends, and gives those people good reasons to distrust him. Military achievement becomes a dangerous qualification for governing when its owner treats disagreement as an insult to be crushed.
